Question: Is it ok to search for a job when you're already in one?
Answer: Yes, in fact the best time to be interviewing is when you already have a job. There is a human bias known as ‘preselection’ which favors candidates who already have a job over unemployed candidates. One can never predict the future - in today’s corporate world, companies have no loyalty to their employees and will have no compunction about laying them off at a moment’s notice, so why should employees be loyal to their employers? Interviewing well is also a skill which requires practice, so it is good to interview periodically to maintain those abilities, even if you are happy in your current job. Finally, just because you are interviewing, doesn’t mean you’re actually going to get an offer (it is a numbers game after all), and if you do get an offer, you don’t have to take it if you don’t want to. Interviewing is also a good way to assess your market value - if you’re getting offers far higher than what you’re currently making, then you are likely being underpaid.

Question: Are there any reactions that can produce only the 1 enantiomer?
Answer: Yes, these are called ‘asymmetric’ or ‘stereoselective’ reactions. These types of reactions are extremely valuable in synthetic organic chemistry, since a lot of molecules of biological relevance (i.e. drug substances or natural products) are single enantiomers. E.g.: Efavirenz, a HIV medication: Off the top of my head, there are a couple of classes of these types of enantioselective reactions. This list is by no means exhaustive, but here are some broad classes: One of the earliest instances of this class of reactions is the Sharpless Epoxidation, which selectively oxidizes the double bond in allylic alcohols to a single enantiomer of the corresponding epoxide: Enantioselectivity is induced by using a specific enantiomer of diethyl tartrate. Prof. Sharpless also developed the asymmetric dihydroxylation (AD) and asymmetric aminohydroxylation (AA) reactions. Due to the significance of these reactions, he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work in chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions in 2001. 2. Chiral C-C bond formation A growing field in modern organic chemistry is organocatalysis, which is concerned with using small organic molecules as catalysts for organic transformations. When using chiral molecules as the catalyst, asymmetry can be induced in the product. An early example of this is the Hajos-Parrish (also Hajos-Parrish-Barbas-List) reaction: This is an intramolecular aldol reaction catalyzed by proline! Note the simplicity of the reaction and the conditions - proline is a common amino acid and both enantiomers are easily available. This reaction is also carried out at room temperature - no fancy conditions required! For his work in developing asymmetric organocatalytic reactions, Prof. List shared the Nobel Prize in chemistry last year (2021)! 3. Asymmetric reductions A famous example in this class is the ‘CBS’ (Corey-Bakshi-Shibata) catalyst, which selectively reduces ketones to a single enantiomer of the secondary alcohol. The catalyst is derived from proline and the reducing agent is borane. The reducing species is an oxazaborolidine that is prepared in a few steps from proline. This is a powerful reduction method and is widely used in complex synthesis in both academia and industry, from the mg scale to the Kg scale. This could also be considered an early example of organocatalysis! This list and the examples here only barely scratches the surface of what has been developed in this area. If you’re interested in learning more, check out the premier journals in chemistry/organic chemistry, including the Journal of the American Chemical Society, Journal of Organic Chemistry, Organic Letters, Angewandte Chemie, and others.

Question: Which is the stronger acid among HF, HCl, and HBr?
Answer: Other answers here have addressed the differences in acidity of the aqueous solutions. However when in their pure forms, HF is actually the strongest acid. Anhydrous HF (aHF) is a superacid, with a Hammett acidity function (Ho) of -15.1. This is because the fluoride ion can be stabilized by other HF molecules as a bifluoride anion (HF2-). Trace amounts of water can disrupt this autoprotonation equilibrium, which is why in aqueous solutions HF behaves as a ‘weak’ acid.

Question: Was earning a Ph.D more difficult 50 years ago?
Answer: Yes…and no. It depends on the field. In chemistry, for instance, literature searching was far more difficult back then, before the internet and digitized publications. You would have to physically go to the library (gasp!) and search for relevant papers by hand. Nowadays, relevant papers can be found in 5–10 minutes in a few clicks. However, the flip side is that the amount of material you’re expected to be familiar with is significantly greater now than 50 years ago, which means students now have to read an order an magnitude more literature than students 50 years ago. When it comes to the experimental side, journals did have easier submission requirements for papers back then compared to now. For instance, see this short JACS communication by Prof. Andrew Streitwieser, when he was still in high school: Chlorination of Fluorene with Sulfuryl Chloride. This would be unthinkable now. Certain disciplines have become mature, which makes coming up with new ideas extremely challenging. This is something I struggled with during my PhD - 99.999% of the time, when I thought I had a novel idea, it turned out that it had already been done. Either that, or if something was unsolved it was due to the sheer difficulty. This was less so 50 years ago. On the other hand, in organic chemistry we do have a lot of cool new technologies that make life easier - separations and purifications can be quickly carried out with UPLC or automated flash chromatography instruments, 2-D NMR is routine, computational chemistry can be done by non-specialists, and the number of reactions in the toolbox is significantly greater now than it was 50 years ago. The actual writing of manuscripts is also much easier now, thanks to personal computers, word processors, and other software.

Question: What is the one piece of advice you’d give to someone who wants to get a PhD in a STEM field?
Answer: Well, firstly if you’re at the PhD level you should know that “STEM” is not a homogeneous term. You can’t lump together disparate subjects like organic chemistry, immunology, particle physics, or statistics together under one banner; each field has its own job market with varying levels of supply and demand. Subjects relating to computer science/programming are seeing extraordinarily strong growth now, and it is not unusual to see PhD students in those fields getting $150k+ offers before graduation. In contrast, fields like chemistry have negative growth. After completing a PhD you’ll need to postdoc for 5–10 years to become employable due to the insane saturation of that market, otherwise you’ll end up unemployed. That being said, the main thing is to do some research into the job market in the field you’re interested in before starting a PhD so you know what you’re getting into. If the job market is weak, then make sure you have a strategy in place for finding work after completing your thesis.

They are generally Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and can contain various substituents (e.g. alkyl groups) and heteroatoms (e.g. N, O, or S). Answer: In the basic sciences (physics, biology, chemistry), due to the overproduction of PhDs and the current glut of PhD scientists in the job market, simply having a PhD is not enough to get any kind of job (in both academia or industry). Most entry-level positions which used to go to PhDs in the past now require postdoctoral experience as well.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How does a STEM PhD holder get their first industry job?
Answer: With great difficulty. Non-facetious answer: Either through their own connections, their advisor’s connections, or applying to job postings online.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: What's your viewpoint on hiring someone without a degree but who is clearly right for the job?
Answer: I have never been involved in hiring, but: if the person is ‘right for the job', then the fact that he/she does not have a degree should be irrelevant, no?

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: What did you learn "the hard way"?
Answer: Getting a job after a degree (B.S., PhD, whatever) is not about what you know, it’s about who you know. These days, having a degree is not considered a major accomplishment like it was in our parents’ generation. Degree holders of any kind are dime a dozen nowadays, and so in order to get your foot in the door and get a interview/job at any company you need connections and someone who can vouch for your skills.

Answer: Not quite the same thing, but I recently had a matchmaker from a dating service contact me through LinkedIn on behalf of a client. That was interesting…

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Which is the most important when pursuing a PhD, the name of your advisor, the name of your institution, your PhD project, or professional networking?
Answer: I would rank them as follows: When you’re applying to jobs outside of academia, you’ll be dealing with recruiters, HR professionals, and industry professionals who may not know about the latest academic research. When they’re looking for candidates to fill open positions, these people will be scanning hundreds or thousands of resumes, and so they’ll be using quick heuristics to determine competence, and one such filter is the name of the institution you attended. If you went to Harvard/Stanford/MIT/Caltech/Berkeley or another top-ranked school, that is likely to catch the recruiter’s eye and keep you from going in the ‘reject’ pile. The name of your advisor or the specific project you worked on in your PhD are of little relevance unless they’re of immediate interest (e.g. the hiring manager has heard of your advisor or is aware of your area of research). In the absence of being able to name-drop top-ranked important institutions on your CV, professional networking can help get you an interview by establishing connections and getting your application into the hands of a hiring manager, as opposed to disappearing into the ‘online black hole’.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can I find postdoctoral in a different research field than my PhD topic?
Answer: I’m going to take a contrarian view from the other answers here and say with great difficulty. Unless the field you’re planning to postdoc in is relatively unsaturated (meaning a lower PhD graduates:positions ratio), convincing a PI that you have the requisite skills to contribute to research in his/her lab is going to be a tough sell. Why would a professor pay a someone a premium (relative to a PhD student) to work in his/her lab if that person has to learn the field from scratch? Postdoctoral positions are supposed to be for training, but due to the oversaturation of PhD’s in a lot of scientific fields, that is no longer the case. PI’s in most universities usually get 10–20 unsolicited e-mails a week inquiring about postdoctoral positions, so they can take their pick of candidates who are most closely aligned to their needs.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Should a postdoc (or a Ph.D. holder) address assistant professors /full professors by their first name?
Answer: Like other people have said, if you’re meeting or addressing someone for the first time, it’s better to err on the side of caution and be respectful by addressing the professor as “Prof. X” or “Dr. Y”. Once the ice is broken, and the professor indicates that he/she prefers to be on a first-name basis, then it is OK to use the first name. I’m using this strategy myself - in all my correspondences with professors regarding postdoc positions, I address everyone as “Prof.”.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Why is it important to add PhD in front of your name if you have a doctorate?
Answer: It isn’t. I have a PhD and leave it off my name on my LinkedIn, business cards, and my resume. It feels odd to have people call me “Dr. so-and-so”. My first boss gave me a valuable lesson - it’s better to not mention that you have a PhD, and leave it to other people to discover. Once they do, their respect for you will only increase, as they learn that not only are you highly educated, but also modest.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can scientific papers have no novel ideas?
Answer: Sure. Some papers can be review articles, which summarize the latest research and developments in a particular field. These are usually written by experts or practitioners in the field, or sometimes by graduate students as a way of getting up to speed with everything that has been done in an area. Since these are summaries of other people’s research, these articles will not contain any novel ideas. In chemistry, Chemical Reviews is an example of a journal that only publishes review articles.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Is it too late to do a PhD when you are in your late 60′s?
Answer: No, it is not. In fact, that’s the age when I would recommend doing a PhD - when you’re old(er) and more or less done with your career, then you can concern yourself with the “life of the mind” and carry out intellectual pursuits for knowledge’s sake. When you’re young, make some money! Doing a PhD when you’re young will not help with financial stability.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How would I know if R programming is for me?
Answer: The only way to know is to try. There are a variety of R courses you can take online - DataCamp and EdX have some good introductory courses you can check out.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Is there a reason why it isn't mandatory to be employed at any job or employment?
Answer: Well, off the top of my head, this would create enormous inefficiencies in the market. It is normal to have a certain level of unemployment in the workforce as people switch from one job to another. This is called frictional unemployment. However, if you mandate that everyone has to have a job, then it is likely that you’ll have people in jobs that are a poor match for their educational background and skills. For example, there might be a highly educated scientist who got laid off from his/her company due to downsizing, and if you mandate that he/she has to have another job immediately afterwards, he/she might end up in another position (e.g. retail, bank teller, or something else) just to have any job at all, and might thereby miss out on the opportunity to look for a better job that fits his/her background.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: I just finished a PhD and want, above all else, a break. Everybody seems worried about my choice. Am I wrong to want this?
Answer: I’ve been there. The PhD process is mentally exhausting and it is good to get some time off so that you can gain perspective and reacclimatize to life outside academia. However, taking a “break” is a risky proposition - you worked hard for a PhD and you don’t want to necessarily jeopardize your chances for getting a good position in academia or industry by having a gap on your resume. A “break” can easily stretch into a two-year hiatus, as it did in my case since getting a job after a PhD is not that easy. That’s why people are worried, but no, you’re not wrong to want this.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How long were you unemployed after getting your PhD?
Answer: Two years. Unfortunately the job market in my field is extremely saturated, which makes employers very picky about who they hire - they’ll prefer to wait for the perfect “purple unicorn” candidate even if I might be available, willing, and otherwise qualified for the job. Here’s a post I made somewhere else when I was in the depth of my job search, back in 2016: It has been about 20 months since I got my PhD in chemistry, and I’m still on the search applying for my first job. It’s been a really emotionally draining, tough ride. Before I graduated, I had heard horror stories from others about the chemistry job market and how brutal it is…but there’s nothing like experiencing it firsthand yourself. There are several major hurdles, which I’ll try and document here. That being said, it seems to me that there’s really only one surefire way to get a job out of school, and that is through campus recruiting. Unfortunately no companies in my area of study (chemistry) came to hire at my university, so that ruled out that approach. The other way is to join a position through a friend’s referral, which works for smaller companies and startups. Applying to big companies is seemingly slower, since the application has to go through several stages – a recruiter (who may or may not know the subject and understand your resume), followed by an interview with the hiring manager (who will be knowledgeable in the domain), and further interviews. I have been told that ‘80% of jobs never get advertised’ and other statistics like that, but those are only relevant for experienced job seekers looking to move laterally; it’s not relevant for fresh graduates looking for their first job. For your first job, you need to play by the company’s rules for applications. Once you get experience and make contacts, then you can get your friends to backdoor you into positions at other companies. At least, that’s my observation. I don’t know what other avenues there are for gaining employment (I should specify that I mean relevant employment that would utilize my education and background; I could always go and be a cashier at a grocery store, but that would be a massive waste of my education and also the taxpayer money that went into funding that education). I’m including this gem as an example to illustrate my point: I applied to this position at BBraun in Irvine in March – on paper, it is a typical Analytical chemist position, and one that I am reasonably well-suited for. The only weird thing is that they explicitly want “Pharmaceutical industry or a relevant post-doc experience of 3-6 years for PhD”, which doesn’t make much sense (but can be chalked up to “credential inflation” in this over-saturated job market). In any case, I was swiftly rejected by the company, but to my surprise, the position is still up, over 6-7 months later! Stuff like this just really infuriates me. Companies like these waste so much time searching for the perfect “purple unicorn” candidate, and then will raise a hue and cry about a “STEM shortage” when they’ve rejected everyone for the most random reasons. EDIT (10/26/2016): This morning, I was greeted with this e-mail from Merck: “Thank you for your interest in Merck. We appreciate you taking the time to pursue career opportunities with us. We have chosen at this time to suspend the search for this position and may reopen the search at a later date”. I applied to this position 2 months ago (August 25, 2016, to be exact), never heard anything back, and then received this notification. Seriously, something is screwy in hiring – has this happened to other people, or is it just me? Also, I honestly think there should be less of a stigma against unemployment – just look at how much time elapses in the job search! The companies are the ones that are slow in getting back to job seekers; in other words, the rate-determining step in the job search is waiting to hear back from companies, which means that individuals should not be held completely responsible for long periods of unemployment if they are applying aggressively. 2ND EDIT (11/16/2016): Yesterday, I got this email from Eli Lilly: “Thank you for your recent inquiry for the Research Scientist-Small Molecule Design and Development-Developability position, requisition #28370BR. The position in which you originally expressed interest has unfortunately been cancelled and was not filled. Please feel free to review current openings and submit your interest accordingly”. At least this position didn’t leave me hanging for that long – I applied to it on 10/13/2016. I’m just completely nonplussed here…

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Am I missing out if I don't date at a young age (12-18)?
Answer: Yes. This is the time to experiment, try things, make mistakes, and hopefully learn from all these experiences. If you don’t date, you won’t have any experiences to draw on when you do end up in a relationship later in life. Everyone has to make mistakes in this area (such as getting into a relationship with someone incompatible) at some point in life, and it is better to make these mistakes when you are younger than when you are older. Dating someone incompatible when you’re young is less “costly” than potentially getting married to someone incompatible when you’re older (which could end up in divorce, but you wouldn’t know ahead of time since you wouldn’t be able to recognize the red flags without prior experience).

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Have your parents advised against dating/relationships, unlike most American parents?
Answer: Yep - my parents are like most typical immigrant Asian parents. When I was a teenager, I was constantly yelled at to study and not think about girls. Now, when I’m older and I actually want to go back to college and study something non-useless (like computer science or business), I’m told “you’ve studied enough and now you should be chasing girls”. The cognitive dissonance is hilarious. When you’re young and full of hormones, that’s when you should be chasing the opposite gender. Education can be done anytime, in my opinion.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Is it better to do a postdoc at a famous university or with a famous postdoc advisor at a state university?
Answer: Go for the famous university - the name of the university matters far more than your advisor’s name. Here’s the thing: when you apply for jobs, the people reading your resume may not always be familiar with your field and know who the important names are. However, a top-ranked university, like Harvard, Stanford, UC Berkeley, MIT, Caltech, Princeton, or CMU will catch the recruiter’s attention and be more likely to get you an interview. I’ve had far too many people tell me to “get lost” because I didn’t have the proper “academic pedigree”, even though my advisor was one of the top scientists in the world. There are famous state universities as well - UC Berkeley, UCLA, University of Michigan, UT Austin, CU Boulder, UNC Chapel Hill, and the University of Washington are very well regarded in several domains.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Why do people leave their luxurious life in the US and go back to India?
Answer: I wouldn't necessarily characterize life in the U.S. as always being more “luxurious” than a life in in India. In India, as with a lot of other developing countries, labor is very cheap. Thus, even middle-class Indian households are used to having domestic help - someone to come to the house everyday to clean the floors, do the laundry, dishes, and other labor-intensive tasks around the home. This is often a huge culture shock for people moving from India to the U.S. - now you have to do all those things yourself. In addition, the cost of living in India is lower than in the U.S. Food is also much more inexpensive - my friends’ minds were blown when they went to India and discovered how inexpensive it is to eat there!

Question: What is the method to convert benzene to phenol?
Answer: This paper (Oxyfunctionalization of hydrocarbons. 14. Electrophilic hydroxylation of aromatics with bis(trimethylsilyl) peroxide/triflic acid) by Prof. George Olah from 1989 provides a one-step method for the electrophilic hydroxylation of aromatics. The use of bis(trimethylsilyl)peroxide and triflic acid provides a homogeneous medium for the one-step oxidation of arenes to phenols. Bis(trimethylsilyl)peroxide (or TMSOOTMS) is in turn prepared from TMSCl, DABCO, and aqueous hydrogen peroxide. However, as other people have mentioned here, the Cumene process is the major industrial process used nowadays; this produces phenol and acetone as coproducts.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can a PhD chemistry pursue her career as business analyst?
Answer: That’s sort of what I am doing right now. After finishing my PhD in chemistry, my first job was at a small strategy consulting company, working as an analyst doing industry and market research. Our industry focus was on the Chemicals, Oil & Gas, Pharmaceutical, and Automotive industries, so it was still somewhat tangentially related to what I had studied. Another option is to just go into general management consulting. Top companies (McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Booz, Strategy&/PWC, LEK Consulting, Accenture, Deloitte, Point B, etc.) do hire PhD’s as management consultants, usually as specialists in their field. From there, you could transition to a role in corporate strategy in a chemicals company, if that’s your thing.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Do I have to be a genius or have a PhD to be a scientist?
Answer: Absolutely not. Grit, perseverance, hard work, and tenacity are much more important qualities for a scientist than being a “genius”. In experimental subjects, luck is often a much larger determinant of success than hard work or intelligence. However, you also need to have the foresight and intellectual preparation to take advantage of luck when it does work out in your favor. This doesn’t require being a genius or having a PhD, just having the domain knowledge to know what’s going on. As Louis Pasteur said, “In the fields of observation chance favors only the prepared mind.”

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can a PhD degree, in a relevant subject, lead to a higher salary and swift promotion in the Corporate World?
Answer: A PhD is a weird degree - it’ll hold you back at the beginning of your career, but towards the end, it will be an invaluable asset. Right after you finish your PhD, you’ll find that you’re overqualified for most entry-level positions, and the few openings there are for PhD’s with 0–2 years of experience will be swamped with thousands of applications due to the massive overproduction of PhDs globally. Getting your first few positions is a difficult struggle. However, towards the mid-to-late career, a PhD can help you get promoted, since companies like having highly educated individuals in the executive team. It helps with corporate image.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can a PhD student afford to live in Los Angeles earning U$ 1700/month?
Answer: My take-home salary on my PhD stipend was about $1800/mo, and I lived in Los Angeles, near USC for 7 years. It’s definitely doable, but it will be a stretch. At the time, I was staying in a small studio apartment and the rent was around $900–950/mo, utilities included. However, it was cheap for a reason - it had cockroaches and I had to suffer through a bedbug infestation for over a year. Even in Southern California, property prices are going up; it’ll help if you can get a roommate to split the rent.

Question: What would you advise a 5th year PhD, with no publications, wanting to pursue an academic career?
Answer: Going into the academic career track with no publications is near impossible. You’ll need to do a postdoc or two to bring your publication record to a decent length, so start looking into that. Think about what your research interests are, and based on that, identify who you would like to work with. Then talk to your professor and learn about his/her network and who his/her contacts are, and see if there is any intersection between the two groups. Hopefully there will be! If not, try networking on your own at conferences and other meetings.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Would it be possible to learn a full programming language only using Codecademy?
Answer: No. Codeacademy teaches you the bare minimum to get you started in programming - it’ll take you from knowing absolutely nothing to getting comfortable with basic syntax and control flow concepts. It was a very useful resource for me when I started learning programming a few years ago. It’s a great place to get your feet wet, and once you have finished their course(s), you’ll need to go to other resources to continue your education - EdX has some really good ones in that regard that can take you to an intermediate level.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: What are the minimum credentials to be considered a legitimate scientist?
Answer: The wonderful thing about science is that you don’t necessarily need formal credentials in order to make a contribution to research. While it does help to have an advanced degree, since that provides you a solid foundation in the field, it is not absolutely necessary. For example, this paper was published by the legendary Andrew Streitweiser while he was in high school, and is a single-author paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society! It is an interesting publication for its time (the 1940’s’). Additionally, Streitweiser criticizes a paper by “Kharasch and Brown” - these are none other than the legendary chemists M. S. Kharasch, the founder of the Journal of Organic Chemistry and a major contributor to free-radical chemistry, and Nobel Laureate H. C. Brown!

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can I tell Ph.D. admission officers at top schools that I want to go into the industry after my Ph.D. and not lower my chances of getting admitted?
Answer: Your future plans after graduation should have no bearing on your admissions decision. In most fields, since the number of academic positions relative to the number of PhD graduates is extremely low (at least in the U.S.), the probability is very low that a PhD student will go into academia anyway. Professors make admissions decisions based on whether or not you will be able to succeed in graduate school and get a PhD, not on your future plans. In any case, the path to a PhD takes a long time, and it is very common that your interests may change during that time. It’s perfectly normal - you may decide during the PhD that you might want to stay in academia after all! Note: Take this with a grain of salt since I have not been on a graduate admissions committee.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: People with jobs in dying industries (industries losing jobs to outsourcing, lack of demand, etc), what's holding you back from moving to a new field?
Answer: The barrier in retraining can can be pretty significant, even for young people. For example, I was unemployed for 2 years after getting a PhD in chemistry — my education and skills were basically obsolete when I graduated. I was trying to transition to “Data Science" during that time, but because my prior education had zero overlap with “Data Science”, it was challenging, and I was discovering that the only way to develop the skills and credibility necessary to become employable in that field would be to get a bachelor's degree in Computer Science. That would require having to apply to colleges again and take the necessary entrance exams again, and I did not have the motivation. Bottom line: it is not as easy to simply switch fields as one might think. It depends strongly on what your prior education and skills are.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Is it a good idea to do a Ph.D. after a master’s in chemistry or to get some experience in the pharma industry and then go for a Ph.D. in pharmaceutics?
Answer: When you’re in the market looking for a job, you’ll learn this truth: Work experience trumps education, 100% of the time. If you have the opportunity to get some work experience under your belt now, do it. The added advantage is that you’ll also make some money. You can always go back to school later if you find you’re hitting a ceiling at work and the degree is necessary for promotion.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: When do chemists decide whether to report 13C NMR data in their paper?
Answer: I don’t know where you’re getting this from - “Most papers report 1H NMR, but do not report 13C NMR data.” This is not true, as far as I know. Most chemistry journals today (at least the ones I have submitted to) require 13C NMR data as part of the characterization for new compounds, in addition to other properties, such as 1H NMR, IR peaks, melting point (if solid), etc.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can we predict what a chemical smell will be like, based on its chemical structure?
Answer: No we can’t, at least not yet. The flip side of this question is that we also do not know the mechanism by which molecules are detected by the nose. There are two competing theories: the “lock-and-key” theory, and the “vibration” theory propounded by Luca Turin. As far as I know, the best place to find information on this topic is this review published over 20 years ago: Structure−Odor Relationships

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Can you get a PhD and MBA during the same time period?
Answer: Yes - I know people who have done it. If you’re doing a PhD, then like others here have said, your #1 priority is research. However, if you can manage your time well, you might be able to take 1 MBA class per quarter or semester outside of your other commitments, and by the time you complete your PhD…you just might have completed enough courses for an MBA as well. This is predicated on a PhD taking much longer to complete than the usual 2 years for an MBA.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How can anyone with a PhD and a master’s be unemployed?
Answer: Why not? This can happen for any number of reasons. A PhD does not make you very desirable to employers. In fact, it does the opposite - a PhD closes a lot more doors than it opens. It happened to me; I was unemployed for 2 years after completing my PhD, stuck in a rather futile job search. Illustrative Example (this happened in the last 24 hours): I’m applying around for jobs now, and found a position that seemed to be a good match. The job description was very general but stated that they wanted a PhD in chemistry with 0–3 years experience. I was able to find someone on LinkedIn to send my resume to the hiring manager. I just heard back - apparently the hiring manager “thought my resume was good, but is looking for a specific skill, and he didn’t say what that was”. The job description does not list much by way of skills, so it is hard to know what the hiring manager is looking for. Unfortunately this is a common scenario with PhD jobs - people become much more specific on the types of skills/competencies they want you to have, which makes it much more difficult to land a position.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Should I put Microsoft Office on my resume?
Answer: If you’re applying to junior positions which list “Microsoft Office” in the job description, then you’ll need to put it in the Skills section in your resume so that it will have a higher probability of getting past the ATS.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How can I get into graduate school for chemistry without a chemistry degree?
Answer: It’ll be difficult, and without an educational background in chemistry, I doubt you will be able to get admitted to any graduate chemistry programs for experimental fields requiring laboratory work, e.g. organic, inorganic, or organometallic chemistry. If you have a background in physics then you might be able to get admitted for physical chemistry, especially if the professors in the department need someone with your skillset. Similarly, if you studied computer science you could get admitted for computational chemistry. Same thing for biology. But really - the chemistry job market sucks now, so if you didn’t study it, consider yourself lucky that you dodged a bullet.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: In thin layer chromatography, does the more polar substance retain in the silica plate or not? I mean, can polar substances move on silica plate?
Answer: Polar substances can move on a silica plate if the solvent system (or eluent) is polar enough to move it along. That’s why you’ll have to experiment with multiple solvent systems when doing a TLC to find the one that gives the best separation between the components in the mixture.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: When picking a college major, should you pick something you're good at but don't particularly like or something you're average at but you love?
Answer: Neither. You pick something that will pay the bills after you graduate. Sorry, but this whole business of “studying what you like” is highly overrated. I loved chemistry, studied it for over 10 years, got a PhD, ended up unemployed for two years, and finally got a job in a unrelated field, meaning all that time, effort and investment has gone to waste. Should have studied computer science— that's where all the money and jobs are today.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How would doing your PhD or Postdoc with a Nobel laureate affect your career?
Answer: Not much. Contrary to what other people think, the name of the school/institute where you do your PhD has a much bigger impact than who your advisor is. If the professor is a recent Nobel Laureate, then it is likely that he/she will have a lot of connections, and these are what will really help get you into academic or industrial positions. These days, if you want to get any kind of position, your advisor needs to pick up the phone and call his/her contacts and say “Hey - my student is looking for a job. You better hire him/her, he/she is really, really good”. All my friends who have gotten positions (either academic or industrial) had advisors who did just that. I did my PhD in a Nobel Prize-winning lab, ended up unemployed for 2 years afterwards, and am now doing work completely unrelated to my area of study. Maybe I’m an extreme outlier, but take from that what you will.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How many PhD students feel that becoming a PhD holder is respectable? It seems that no one gives PhD holders or professors any respect.
Answer: Here’s the thing: Education alone won’t get you respect - it’s what you do with your education that will earn it. If you’re doing a PhD just to earn respect, then stop. There are other much easier ways to gain “respect”.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Is it rude to find the email for a hiring manager and contact them directly? I have no contact at this company. I just applied on LinkedIn, but also found the hiring manager's email from an old Tweet of theirs.
Answer: When I started my job search, I used to think it was rude to email strangers directly - after all, we’re all inundated with useless emails and hate seeing spam or junk email in our inbox. However, I have started contacting hiring managers directly, and guess what - it’s literally like unlocking a cheat code, and I’m now getting a lot more callbacks for interviews than ever before! You can usually figure out who the hiring manager is (not the recruiter, they are different people) from the posted job description. You may have to do some sleuthing using LinkedIn or other tools and make sure you’re using the right keywords (e.g. “director/manager” of the group in the company you’re applying to). You can then send the person a message (InMail) through LinkedIn, but LinkedIn is often ignored. E-mail is a better bet, as those are much less likely to be ignored. Question: What is it like to defend a doctoral dissertation in front of a committee?
Answer: Some of the answers here are really dramatic, which I find interesting. Giving your PhD defense should be like giving any other talk, and hopefully you should have plenty of experience talking about your work from group meetings, seminars, conferences, and other events. Since it is your research, you should know it inside out by that point and be able to talk about it in your sleep. By the time your defense rolls around, you are expected to be the authority on the subject matter, not your advisor, so that should give you a degree of confidence. A doctoral defense is usually open to the public - the department will put out flyers and other notifications announcing it, and your thesis committee (consisting of your advisor, some professors from your department, and an external examiner outside your department/school as well) will be in attendance, sitting in the front and asking questions to make sure you have the requisite level of knowledge to be awarded the PhD title. The defense is not the big hurdle in getting the degree, it’s simply the last step and the one that is the most well known since it is open to the public. The major step is passing the PhD candidacy or qualifying exam(s), which take place earlier on, usually in the 2nd or 3rd year. By the time you’re ready to defend, you and your advisor should have worked together to iron out the kinks in your research. The defense is almost like a formality, where everyone can see what you’ve worked so hard on for the last several years. It is exceedingly rare for someone to fail at the defense stage, because that also makes your advisor look bad. What is more likely is that if some parts of the thesis are weak, you might be asked to go back and work on them some more, and have the committee review it again before you officially submit it. The exciting part is not the defense itself, but the celebrations afterward. (Photo taken after my defense)

Question: How long does medicine stay in my system?
Answer: This is what the field of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) addresses. Within this area, there is a group of concepts known as “ADME”, which stand for: Adsorption covers all the different ways a drug molecule can enter your body - orally, nasally, intravenously, or transdermally, or even rectally (as a suppository!) for example. Distribution refers to how the drug molecule transports itself from the site of entry to the target location in the body. This is where we see that even with all our understanding of medicine, we’re still at a very nascent stage of understanding - in order to get the compound where it needs to go, we just load up the bloodstream and hope that takes it there! Distribution models often divide up the body into compartments - the single-compartment model is the simplest, but more can be added, which adds accuracy but also introduces calculational complexity. Metabolism is concerned with how the molecule is broken down in vivo. Molecules in the body are broken down by all kinds of enzymes, and sometimes these products (also called metabolites) can be more active (in a good or bad way) in vivo than the parent molecule. Sometimes a molecule can be designed such that it is only active until it has been cleaved by an enzyme in the blood, liver, or stomach, and these are referred to as prodrugs. Excretion - how does it leave your body? Either through the urine (which means it has to get renally cleared via the kidneys) or through feces. So there’s no one answer for the question “how long does medicine stay in my system?”. It depends on the drug and a host of other personal factors (genetics, diet, lifestyle, etc.). This is why clinical trials are so important when developing new medications.

Question: What does fluoroantimonic acid look like and what are some interesting properties of it?
Answer: I have used fluoroantimonic acid (commonly referred to as “HF-SbF5”) a few times during my PhD research. Unfortunately I never took any photos of it that I could post here :/ It is a clear, colorless liquid formed by mixing anhydrous HF and SbF5 in the appropriate proportions, depending on the strength you need. Making it richer in SbF5 will serve to increase the acidity, but will also make the acid system a stronger oxidant. It fumes strongly in air, because the acid vapors immediately protonate the water molecules in air - what you observe as fumes is actually clouds of the hydronium salt! The wikipedia page mentioned in the other answer here has a lot of useful information about this substance. Because it contains HF, it cannot be stored in glass, and must be stored in PTFE containers. For NMR experiments, PTFE tubes or quartz NMR tubes can be used (at low temperatures), although the quartz will slowly be attacked over time and will have to be discarded after a few uses. HF-SbF5 is one of the strongest Bronsted acids known in chemistry and can protonate just about anything. It can be used for making stable solutions of carbocations or other types of cations, which can then be studied spectroscopically, using NMR or Raman spectroscopy.

Question: Should one email professors when one is looking for postdoc positions?
Answer: E-mail is the most common method for contacting professors for post-doc positions. Some professors may be old fashioned and insist only on “snail-mail” applications. I’ve seen cases where people meet prospective supervisors at conferences or other places, chat with them in person, and then get an offer that way. I have also seen postdoctoral positions being advertised on Job Search | Indeed or C&EN jobs. If you’re contacting a professor about a potential postdoc position over e-mail, you would e-mail them a cover letter explaining clearly your background, what you can contribute, and what you hope to gain, in addition to a CV and research summary. Question: Why do you always have to do the same job as past experience on your resume? Why can't someone change their career?
Answer: The answer to your first question is largely due to two factors: In a highly competitive job market, hiring managers will often become extremely risk-averse, because they can afford to be picky and choose the perfect candidate out of the applicant pool. The software is not smart enough to consider applicants who would be able to do the job just fine even if their experience and education is not a 100% match to the requirements. Changing career paths is possible, but it requires someone to take a chance on you and is largely a function of how well you can convince the potential employer to take you on. This is usually easier after you’ve worked for a few years and developed a network and “transferable” skills.

I would think mental illness would be the least of your worries here.

Question: How do fracked wells tend to generate more wastewater?
Answer: It’s not so much that a fracked well inherently produces wastewater, but the hydraulic fracturing process itself that produces a lot of wastewater (called produced water in Oil & Gas lingo). Source: Chemical & Engineering News Hydraulic fracturing involves pumping millions of gallons of fracturing fluid (which is 99% water) into the ground in order to reduce the porosity of the shale or other hydrocarbon-containing rocks, thereby enhancing the flow of oil and improving hydrocarbon recovery. All the water that is injected into the ground has to go somewhere - some of it might stay underground but the majority will come back out along with the recovered oil/gas. This wastewater will contain a variety of impurities, including organics, inorganics, and even radioactive minerals. Treating this water is very expensive, and the service companies will often prefer to dispose of this water by injecting it deep underground. As a result, Earthquakes in Kansas have surged as a result of oil and gas production.

Question: Would professors of top schools ever hire a postdoc with a PhD from a lower ranked university?
Answer: Yes, this does happen, but you have to sell yourself very well and hope that your PI (or others in your department who may know you and have connections to higher ranked schools) will vouch for you and write glowing recommendations. Story time: I knew a member of our chemistry department who published 0 papers during his/her PhD and gave an extremely mediocre thesis defense (I say this because another professor who attended the defense and was not on the student’s committee, was tearing it apart for a good half an hour afterwards). Nonetheless, the student was allowed to graduate, and to everyone’s surprise, was able to secure an extremely competitive postdoctoral appointment at a Nobel Prize winner’s lab at a top university! Witnessing these events caused me to lose faith in the belief that academia is a meritocracy.

Question: Why do PhD degree holders outside of academia typically not use "Dr." before their names?

In my first job out of my PhD I have been exposed to so much that I would never have otherwise learned remaining in academia. Things like soft skills, market research, clear communication, teamwork, empathy, project management, and other skills are normally picked up on the job, and not in school. The aforementioned stereotypes do have some existence in reality - stereotypes, after all, are not formed in a vacuum.

Question: What is the deal if someone graduated with a PhD from a prestigious school, as opposed to an average school?
Answer: Prestigious or well-known schools will give you a massive boost in the job market. Having a name like “Harvard”, “Stanford”, “Princeton”, “MIT”, “Caltech”, or “Berkeley” on your resume/CV will open up so many more doors for you that would otherwise have remained closed if you didn’t attend those schools. Well-known schools will have a lot more companies who will come to recruit graduates, and professors at top institutions are more likely to have connections with companies that will help in landing you that elusive first job after graduation. I did my PhD at a lower-ranked institution, and we had zero companies coming to recruit students from our department. The sad thing is that even though there may be negligible differences between PhD students at various institutions (in terms of domain knowledge, skill, or work ability), a lot of employers will prefer students from the aforementioned prestigious schools, due to brand recognition. It’s the same reason why you would prefer to wear a Hugo Boss suit or buy a Hermes bag rather then get some cheap knockoff.

Question: What do PhD students do if they graduate without any journal publications?
Answer: I’ve said this in several places, and I’ll say it again: Some of the most brilliant, hard-working, dedicated, and knowledgeable scientists I’ve had the privilege of working with got zero publications during their PhDs. Number of publications is a poor metric for determining research productivity, but it is the only one we’ve got, unfortunately. Success in experimental fields is largely dependent on randomness or luck - you may get lucky and find what you’re looking for quickly, in only a few trials, and be able to write it up and publish it. The worst case (and usual) scenario is that you probably won’t find what you’re looking for, even after 1000’s of trials, and therefore won’t be able to publish anything. Does that say anything about your knowledge of the subject matter or skills as a scientist? No. If the student is hell-bent on academia and getting a tenure-track faculty position, then he/she will have to do a postdoc or two in order to beef up the CV and build up a publication list in order to become a competitive candidate. The number of publications, number of first-author publications, and the length of your CV are metrics that are only relevant when you are applying for academic tenure-track faculty positions. A lot of industrial positions do not care about publications as much as competence, which as I mentioned above, does not necessarily correlate with publishing ability.

Question: What does it feel like to be an unemployed PhD?
Answer: It sucks. One major challenge is dealing with the constant cognitive dissonance you’ll face - in the media and in society, you’ll be bombarded by messages that say “we have a shortage of skilled scientists!” or “STEM careers are the greatest!”. However, once you actually try applying to jobs, you’ll see a very different picture that goes unacknowledged: that we have a legitimate surplus of highly-skilled and highly-qualified scientists competing for a vanishingly small number of academic and industrial positions, and the ratio of job seekers:positions available is only getting worse. Large pharma companies like Merck or Pfizer may get 3000–4000 PhD applicants for an open position. In addition, pivoting or otherwise transitioning to a different field from the one you did your PhD in is not that easy. The exception is if your work involved programming of some kind; those PhDs are being heavily recruited by Wall Street as “quants” and by other tech companies as “Data Scientists”. If, like me, your research involved zero programming, you might find it is difficult to start learning a new subject from scratch, especially one that has little in common with what you were working so hard on for the past decade or so. Your mental energy may be drained but you’ll have to somehow manage to summon the willpower to soldier on.

Question: Why can't we generate more helium using some advanced form of physical chemistry?
Answer: Because helium (and other elements) are not generated through chemical means. Elements are synthesized through physical means, which involves either the fusion of nuclei (which happens in stars and supernovae) or the fission of nuclei (e.g. the decay of heavy elements such as uranium). The majority of the helium in the universe exists in the stars and is formed through interstellar fusion, whereas all the helium on earth is generated from the alpha decay of heavy elements. Chemistry is the domain that involves processes for generating molecules or breaking them down into constituent elements or atoms. Physics involves the synthesis of elements (through fusion or fission of nuclei).

Question: Can I do a master's in organic chemistry even if my specialization is in statistics, or any other subject?

Question: What are the main reasons why PhD candidatures extend to 4-6 years so I can prevent this from happening?
Answer: The Ph.D. degree can take a long time because it is a research degree. Research is by nature a very stochastic process, and you cannot predict when you will get useful results or when a discovery will be made. It takes time to achieve the necessary knowledge and obtain complete domain expertise in the area you’re working in, but this is not the difficult part. The difficult part is generating new knowledge and adding to the existing corpus of humanity’s collective knowledge in your field of interest. If you’re dead set on finishing a PhD in x number of years, your best bet is to interview many professors or potential PhD advisors until you find someone who says that they will only support you for those x number of years. There was one professor in the department in which I did my PhD who would only support his students for 5 years, and so they would have to finish the degree and leave within that time. There are pros and cons associated with that, but that is a topic for another discussion.

Question: How can a graduate student make the best out of his/her PhD experience?
Answer: Remember that while you’re a PhD student, the university is actually covering your tuition (at least in the U.S.). So don’t be afraid to take advantage of that and take classes in other areas you’re interested in. A smart strategy is to take 1 class or so every semester on the side; by the time you graduate, you may have enough credits for a master’s in another subject! I know a couple of people who have actually done this; my uncle got an MBA while working towards a Ph.D. in computer science, and a friend of mine who worked in the lab adjacent to mine during my PhD managed to get a master’s in computer science along with his PhD in chemistry by surreptitiously taking 1 or 2 CS courses every semester. The other thing to remember is that networking is probably the most important thing you can do; while working in the lab, learning the subject, and publishing papers is important, ultimately you’ll only be able to secure academic or industrial positions through the strength of your networks. Weird as it may sound…getting a job these days has very little to do with your skills and competencies, and has a lot more to do with who you know. Bottom line: Slaving away in the lab for hours, months, or years may get you results in your research, but it won’t necessarily help you once you graduate and are out in the world looking for a job.

Question: Is it true that some vegetarians/vegans truly get sick from the lack of meat?

Question: How did Ph.D students become so good at writing?
Answer: Please don’t generalize; I have known a lot of Ph.D. students who were objectively terrible writers. That being said… As others here have mentioned, practice is a big component. I would also imagine that growing up in an English-speaking country and attending English-medium schools would also help a lot. Any writer worth his or her salt will also tell you that reading a lot is extremely important; that’s how you learn about acceptable conventions, idioms, flow, and what works in the domain you’re interested in. Getting timely and constructive feedback from other good writers is also invaluable; this is a critical step in being able to grow as a writer, as it is right there that others will point out the good and bad elements in your writing. Also, keep in mind that a lot of what you read that is written by Ph.D.s (e.g. scientific articles, reviews, books, chapters, etc.) will probably have been edited hundreds of times before publication, so is more likely to be a group rather than solo effort.

Question: What is the purpose of a PhD?

You’ve done additional courses of study, as well as original research which has contributed to the collective corpus of humanity’s knowledge. Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: Does the amount of working hours of PhD students correlate with the number of published journal articles?
Answer: Absolutely not! Experimental research is often a very stochastic endeavor. You’re operating on the frontiers of science, where the outcomes of the experiments you’re running are essentially unknown, and you’re guessing (or hypothesizing, according to the scientific method) what the result will be. It’s basically a fancy way of throwing a bunch of darts and seeing which ones will stick. You could get lucky and find what you’re looking for very quickly, or (and this is the most common situation) you could spend years (and lots of money) searching futilely with no luck. Some of the most hard-working scientists I have known have 0 papers to their name, while I’ve known some other clueless people who have fancy publications simply by being in the right place at the right time.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: If almost everyone can learn programming for free, why is the salary relatively very high?
Answer: This is an easy question to answer. It’s easy to get started learning programming - like you and others here have mentioned, a lot of major languages (Python, Ruby, JavaScript, R, C++, and others) are open source, which means they are free to use. IDE’s/text editors are also freely available, and there are hundreds of courses online that can teach you programming in a variety of languages from a complete novice level (starting with “Hello World!”) to fairly advanced concepts, such as Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence, completely for free. The only costs you’ll incur are those involved with obtaining a computer to program on, and maintaining an internet connection. However, getting to a level of proficiency in programming where you’ll be employable is not so trivial, especially if you’re self-teaching. This requires a level of persistence and tenacity beyond what you would need if you were simply taking CS courses in a college/university. If you’re self-learning, you don’t have anybody to hold your hand and walk you through problems and solutions. You also don’t necessarily have the benefit of a guided curriculum so that you can have some structure in your learning. Making projects is a big deal nowadays; employers want to see tangible proof of your skills, and making something from scratch is not as trivial as it sounds. It’s pretty daunting to start with a blank screen on an IDE and build something from there. While there may be millions of people who start to learn programming at any given point, only a handful of people actually stick with it and end up developing employable skills.

Question: Is it necessary to learn Python in the duration to earn a PhD?

Question: How do organic chemists prepare sodium hydride for reaction?
Answer: I used both the NaH and KH suspensions a couple of times during my PhD for some synthetic preparations, and it is fairly straightforward - the main thing to keep in mind is that they can react extremely vigorously with water (releasing heat and a fire!), so you want to maintain anhydrous conditions. In addition, KH and NaH are both sensitive to oxidation by air, so you want to exclude oxygen as much as possible. The bottle the NaH/KH suspension is sold in will tell you the % by mass of KH/NaH, with the remainder being mineral oil. The suspension itself can be handled safely under air, although you still want to minimize exposure to reduce oxidation. Vortex the bottle to make sure everything is as evenly mixed as possible, and then quickly weigh out how much you need into a clean, dry, tared flask (Schlenk flask if possible). For example, if you need 1 g of NaH and the suspension is 40% by mass, then you would need 2.5 g of the suspension. Depending on the reaction, you could then use the KH/NaH as is - since mineral oil mixes with all alkane solvents, if alkanes are spectators in your reaction, you could just add the alkane solvent and you should be good to go. However, if solubility is an issue (which it usually is with NaH/KH), then you may need to wash out the mineral oil. In order to do that, mix the suspension with pentane/hexane/petroleum ether, swirl it for a bit under nitrogen/argon, let it settle completely, and then carefully drain the supernatant liquid under nitrogen/argon. Repeat this procedure 5–6 times to quantitatively remove the mineral oil, and then dry the resulting gray solid with light vacuum. Flush the flask again with nitrogen/argon and you should be good to go.

Question: Does a PhD title open more occupational opportunities? I am in a Neuroscience PhD program, looking for a job as a Data Scientist. I might quit, and take a data analyst position, for more experience. Would I be better with more experience and no PhD?
Answer: As someone who earned a PhD in organic chemistry and was repeatedly rejected in over 1000+ job applications in a rather futile 2 year job search, my answer is: a PhD title, by itself, closes a lot more more occupational opportunities than it opens. The exception is of course certain fields where you have desirable “transferable skills” (I hate that term), such as Physics, mathematics, electrical engineering, biostatistics, and other fields. These PhDs are sought after by banks and hedge funds to work as “quants” developing financial models, or by tech companies as “Data Scientists”, gleaning actionable insights from volumes of data. Whether you need a PhD or not depends on the field; a PhD can be a burden when trying to get a career started, but then become an asset later on. In some companies, only employees with PhDs will be promoted beyond a certain level, which is why it may be useful to get one. With regards to “Data Science”, a lot of recruiters and companies seem to still have an unhealthy obsession for candidates with relevant advanced degrees (keyword being relevant), so it might be worth sticking around to get the PhD, but simultaneously take CS courses at your university (and online) on the side, and do independent projects that you can show to prospective employers to demonstrate your programming chops.

Question: What are the best data science courses on edX?
Answer: I still haven’t taken that many courses on EdX (only 10 or so), and I’m still a bit of a novice at programming and Data Science. The only real “Data Science” course I have managed to complete on EdX so far is Microsoft DAT210x: Programming with Python for Data Science. Microsoft DAT210x Course Info | edX is a decent introduction to machine learning and the scikit-learn module in Python. I took the course last year as a supplement to a “Data Science” bootcamp I was also enrolled in at the time, and the course really helped with gaining more understanding of the algorithms (KNN, K-Means, Random Forest, etc.) and other related topics (e.g. dimensionality reduction with PCA and isomap). I found it to be a challenging course, and I spent more than the recommended 4–8 hours/week on the programming assignments. They were all really interesting, and challenging enough where I didn’t get completely frustrated and give up. We used PCA and Isomap to project 3-D images into 2-D space, K-Means to identify people’s residences based on anonymized geolocation data from their cellphones (!), linear regression to reconstruct audio samples (sort of like what they do on TV shows!), SVC to analyze whether or not someone has Parkinson’s based on collected speech quality, and other interesting examples. DAT210x gives a good introduction to the Pandas and Scikit-learn libraries. The course could use a little more polish (there were typographical errors all over the place), but I’m sure those issues will be fixed in future iterations. The explanations for some of the concepts (such as PCA, Isomap, and K-means) were a bit wishy-washy, but that is the challenge of having a course like this for a general audience; you don’t know if the people taking this would necessarily have the background in Linear Algebra to understand the math behind these concepts. If you’re curious about the programming assignments, I’m posting them in my github.

Question: Are CF2 and CCl2 real chemical compounds?
Answer: To build on Mark B Fischer’s answer, difluorocarbene and dichlorocarbene (CF2 and CCl2) can be generated during reactions, but since their lifetimes are very short, they cannot be isolated and stored. Carbenes are rather reactive, and once formed, will react with other electron donors/acceptors or dimerize/oligomerize with themselves. It’s pretty easy to form difluorocarbene or dichlorocarbene; a common way is to generate the trihalo carbanion (by deprotonation of chloroform or CF3H with KOtBu or similar bases), which then undergoes α-dehalogenation to give the dihalocarbene.

Question: What is the best way for a PhD student to invest their (small) salary?
Answer: As Prof. Burton Malkiel discusses in his excellent book A Random Walk Down Wall Street, one of the best ways for anyone (not just PhD students) to invest in the markets is simply to put your money into index funds, such as those provided by Vanguard. It is difficult to beat the market due to the “efficient market hypothesis”, which states that all available information is reflected in a stock’s price; while you may think you have some special knowledge that a particular stock is going to go up at the time of purchase, on the other end, the seller probably thinks that he/she is smart for thinking that the stock may go down! In A Random Walk Down Wall Street, Burton Malkiel begins by comparing a $10,000 investment in the S&P 500 index fund to the same amount in the average actively-managed mutual fund. From the start of 1969 through to June 30, 1998, the index investor was ahead by almost $140,000: her original $10,000 increased 31 times to $311,000, while the active-fund investor ended up with only $171,950.

Question: Is there a shortage of STEM workers in the US or not? I keep reading that it’s just a ruse to bring in cheap H1B labor, and US workers are forced to train their replacements (e.g. Disney).

However, as a chemist, and as someone who would fit into the “S” (for “Science”) in “STEM”… there is no shortage, but a massive, massive glut. I was unemployed for 2 years after getting my PhD in a rather futile job search as I learned this the hard way. This glut primarily manifests itself by companies (and hiring managers) becoming extremely picky in choosing between qualified candidates, often rejecting candidates who are not from Harvard/Stanford/MIT/Caltech (even if they may be perfectly qualified or even overqualified) or favoring H-1 applicants because they cannot leave the company (I was told this off the record by several people). Question: Can I graduate PhD without publication?
Answer: Yes. Some of the brightest, most knowledgeable, hardworking, intelligent, and experienced scientists I have had the privilege of working with graduated from their PhDs in chemistry with zero publications. As Nassim Nicholas Taleb (author) talks about in his excellent book The Black Swan, scientific research is the pursuit of “lumpy outcomes”. Obtaining results is highly dependent on randomness or luck, especially since publishers only care about “publishable”, i.e. positive results. You may get lucky and find what you’re looking for after a few iterations, or you may be really unlucky and not find what you were looking for in your lifetime, after millions of iterations! And then someone else might come along and discover what you were trying so hard to find completely by accident, and then take all the credit for it. On the flip side, I knew a member of our chemistry department who published 0 papers during his/her PhD and gave an extremely mediocre thesis defense (I say this because another professor who attended the defense and was not on the student’s committee, was tearing it apart for a good half an hour afterwards). Nonetheless, the student was allowed to graduate, and to everyone’s surprise, was able to secure an extremely competitive postdoctoral appointment at a Nobel Prize winner’s lab! A year later, another friend of mine, who was praised unanimously by everyone in our department as being a “rock star of organic chemistry”, was turned down by the very same professor when he/she applied for a postdoctoral position there, even though this student had published 20+ papers in excellent journals, including a couple of reviews and book chapters. Witnessing these events caused me to lose faith in the belief that academia is a meritocracy.

Question: Who are some of the smartest people in chemistry?
Answer: The title of “smartest chemist ever” would probably belong to the legendary Prof. Robert Burns Woodward. Woodward had a natural affinity for chemistry, especially organic chemistry, from an early age. He used to read the German chemical literature even before he joined MIT for college, and later received his PhD in chemistry from MIT just one year after completing his bachelor’s degree! Woodward revolutionized the practice of organic chemistry by demonstrating that it was indeed possible to synthesize basically any molecule by breaking it down into pieces and planning the synthesis of each piece based on rational thought and known chemical principles. His influence is still felt today, so much so, that organic chemists often say that we are in the “Post-Woodwardian” age of organic chemistry. Woodward is also probably the only person who could lay claim to three Nobel Prizes. He received the Prize in 1965 for “his outstanding achievements in the art of organic synthesis”, and would have also shared the Prize in 1981 with Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui for the development of Frontier Molecular Orbital theory and the eponymous “Woodward-Hoffmann rules”. When Wilkinson and Fischer received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for their work in organometallic chemistry (specifically “sandwich” compounds), Woodward was incensed and wrote a strongly worded letter to the Nobel committee, in which he castigated them for overlooking his contributions to the development of this field. Woodward insisted that he had suggested the now-accepted “sandwich” structure of Ferrocene after Wilkinson, at the time a junior faculty member at Harvard, had approached him (Woodward) for help with interpreting and deciphering the characterization data of the orange powder. I could go on and on, but this will do for now… EDIT (4/10/2017): A nice article from this week’s issue of C&EN: Remembering organic chemistry legend Robert Burns Woodward

Question: Should I get a PhD if I don't want to work in Academia?
Answer: Answer: Only if the exact career you want requires a PhD. Otherwise it is not worth it, in my opinion. You should also do some research into the job market in the particular area you are interested in, and get a realistic idea of the career progression and how difficult it may (or may not be) to land a job after finishing a PhD/postdoc. Another important item to look into is whether “postdoc-ing” is common in your field, which will also affect the degree of saturation of the job market and how you should go about getting an industry job. For instance, in the sciences (in chemistry at least), thanks to the glut of PhDs, there is also a large number of postdocs competing for a vanishingly small number of positions in both industry and academia. Job postings advertised for fresh PhDs with 0–3 years experience will get swamped by desperate postdocs with anywhere from 2–10 years of post-PhD experience, crowding out the PhD graduates. This is something I experienced firsthand while desperately applying for industry R&D positions after completing my PhD in chemistry. Even though I hate the term “transferable skills”, that is also something to keep in mind in case you are not able to get a foot in the door in your desired field. PhDs with strong quantitative skills (i.e. who also have a strong background, expertise, and experience with mathematics, statistics, and programming) can be gainfully employed in finance and in the tech sector as “data scientists”.
